expected_points: Set clear savings targets, preferably in dollars, and let each manager choose whom to let go.

answer.summary: Mochary recommends setting clear savings targets, delivering each layoff privately through the person’s manager, and offering both departing employees and the remaining team direct, compassionate support. He advises making one deep cut rather than repeated rounds, then listening individually to the stay team’s concerns.

sections.heading: Plan the cuts
sections.content: Bring the managers into an inner circle and tell them how much must be saved. Set dollar targets rather than asking only for a number of people: otherwise, managers may choose the cheapest, most junior employees, who may be doing much of the work. Let each manager choose within their team rather than having department heads dictate specific people; Mochary says this can take about 48 hours.

sections.heading: Tell departing employees one-on-one and offer help
sections.content: Have each person’s manager invite them to a private conversation, ideally in a concentrated morning of back-to-back meetings. Deliver the news face-to-face, acknowledge that it is painful, and give the person room to share their feelings. If there is not time to talk then, offer another hour the next day or soon after. Mochary also describes becoming the departing person’s agent: helping them identify an ideal role and create or land it, including helping someone pursue starting a company. He warns that email, group chats, or announcing layoffs in a group feel dehumanizing and prevent people from expressing their emotions.

sections.heading: Support the remaining team
sections.content: Hold an all-hands with the stay team that afternoon, explain what happened, and answer questions—especially fears about whether more cuts are coming, whether the company is in trouble, and whether people received performance feedback. Mochary recommends cutting deeply enough to avoid repeated rounds, which he says can create organizational trauma. Then have each remaining employee meet one-on-one with their manager for an hour. The manager’s job is to ask about the person’s thoughts and feelings and reflect back what they hear, so the person feels understood. Mochary says this does not erase emotion, but can reduce it enough to help prevent rash quitting or disengagement and support recovery.

answer.summary: Set clear dollar-saving targets, let each manager choose whom to release, and communicate the news privately in a manager-led one-on-one. Offer departing employees practical career help, then address the remaining team’s fears in an all-hands and follow-up one-on-ones.

sections.heading: Plan the cuts
sections.content: Bring the managers into an inner circle and tell them the savings required. Give each manager a dollar target rather than a headcount target: Mochary says a people target can encourage cutting the cheapest, often most junior people, while the actual goal is to save dollars. Let each manager choose whom to let go rather than assigning names from above; he says this decision can take about 48 hours. He also recommends cutting deeply enough to avoid repeated rounds, which he says can traumatize the organization.

sections.heading: Deliver the news humanely and help departing employees
sections.content: Have the person’s manager deliver the news in a private one-on-one—not by email, group chat, or in front of others—so the employee can express their emotions. Managers can schedule these conversations close together on implementation morning. Be direct and compassionate, acknowledge that the news is horrible, and offer a separate hour the next day or later to listen and help. Mochary’s approach is to act as the employee’s agent: learn what they are good at and passionate about, then help them find, create, or land a role where those strengths are needed. For a large layoff, he says managers can do this for their own reports; in his example, a manager with 12 reports could support up to six if no more than half are let go at a time.

sections.heading: Support the remaining team
sections.content: Hold an afternoon all-hands for the stay team: explain what happened and answer their fears, including whether more cuts are coming, whether the company is failing, and whether the affected employees had received feedback. Mochary recommends reassuring the team when true that the cuts were deep enough to happen once and that the remaining people are the team moving forward. Then have each manager meet individually with every remaining team member for an hour, mainly to invite them to share their thoughts and feelings and reflect back what they hear. He says this does not erase the emotions, but can reduce them enough to help people avoid rash reactions and recover.

sections.heading: Expected effects and caveat
sections.content: Mochary says that, in his experience, this follow-up can help the company perform better within two weeks, while without it recovery may take longer; he also says even a poorly handled layoff may be followed by improved performance within two months, but recovery takes longer. These are his reported experiences, not guarantees.
